title: What Are Suprasegmentals and Why Do They Matter?
brief: Define suprasegmentals as the features of spoken language that operate above the level of individual sounds — specifically word stress, sentence stress, rhythm, and intonation. Explain that while individual sounds (vowels and consonants) are important, errors in suprasegmentals are more likely to cause a breakdown in communication or make a speaker sound unnatural to a native-English-speaking listener. Use a simple example to illustrate: show how the same string of words spoken with different stress or intonation can produce entirely different meanings or social effects. Clarify that this unit focuses on these three interconnected layers — stress, rhythm, and intonation — and that mastering them helps learners sound fluent rather than merely accurate.

title: Word Stress: Which Syllable Gets the Beat?
brief: Explain that every English word of more than one syllable has one syllable that receives primary stress — it is louder, longer, and higher in pitch than the others. Provide clear written examples using capital letters or bold to mark the stressed syllable: PHOto / phoTOgraphy / phoTOgraphic, and PREsent (noun) / preSENT (verb), showing how stress can shift meaning entirely. Note that English stress is not always predictable from spelling, which is why learners must learn stress as part of a word's entry in their mental lexicon. Include a short set of everyday example words across two and three syllables — such as TEAcher, baNAna, unDERstand — so the section writer can illustrate the concept concretely without relying on any external source.

title: Sentence Stress: Highlighting What Matters
brief: Explain that in connected speech, not every word receives equal stress: content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs) typically carry stress, while function words (articles, prepositions, auxiliary verbs, pronouns) are usually unstressed and reduced. Show how the placement of the main stress within a sentence — called the nucleus or tonic stress — shifts meaning. Use a single sentence repeated with stress on different words to demonstrate: 'SHE didn't take my bag' vs. 'She didn't TAKE my bag' vs. 'She didn't take MY bag' — each version implies a different contrast or correction. Emphasise that speakers use sentence stress deliberately to signal new information, contrast, or emphasis, and that learners who stress every word equally sound robotic and are harder to follow.

title: Rhythm and Stress-Timing: The Pulse of English
brief: Introduce the concept of stress-timing: in English, stressed syllables tend to occur at roughly regular intervals, regardless of how many unstressed syllables fall between them. This gives English its characteristic 'bouncy' rhythm. Contrast this with syllable-timed languages (where each syllable takes roughly equal time), noting that learners from such language backgrounds often transfer that even rhythm into English, making them harder to understand. Explain the role of weak forms and reduction: function words like 'to', 'and', 'of', and 'can' are typically reduced in natural speech (e.g., 'going to' becomes 'gonna', 'can' becomes /kən/). Provide a written example sentence — such as 'I want to go to the shops' — and show how it sounds in careful speech versus natural connected speech, marking which syllables are stressed and which are reduced.

title: Intonation: The Melody of Meaning
brief: Explain that intonation refers to the rise and fall of pitch across an utterance, and that English uses intonation to signal a range of meanings beyond the words themselves. Cover the two most fundamental patterns: falling intonation (used for statements, wh-questions, and commands — signalling that the speaker has finished and is certain) and rising intonation (used for yes/no questions and to signal that more is coming, or to invite a response). Then introduce the fall-rise pattern, which signals reservation, doubt, or a polite contradiction — for example, saying 'It's quite good' with a fall-rise suggests 'but not perfect'. Use written arrows or descriptions (e.g., 'voice rises on the last stressed syllable') to make the patterns visible on the page. Stress that the same words with different intonation can shift a sentence from a genuine question to a sarcastic comment or a warm invitation.

title: Teaching Suprasegmentals in the Classroom
brief: Offer practical, source-grounded guidance for TEFL teachers on how to make stress, rhythm, and intonation visible and teachable. Suggest techniques such as: clapping or tapping the rhythm of a sentence to feel the stress pattern; using a simple marking system on the board (underlining stressed syllables, drawing arrows for intonation); drilling minimal-stress pairs like 'I DIDN'T steal it' versus 'I didn't STEAL it' to sharpen learner awareness; and using back-chaining to build up sentences from the end so learners absorb the natural rhythm. Remind teachers that learners need both awareness (noticing) and production practice, and that correcting suprasegmental errors gently — by modelling the correct version rather than simply saying 'wrong' — keeps the communicative flow of a lesson intact. Keep all examples original and classroom-ready.
